```{r, include = FALSE}
options(width = 100)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
```

AgriDesign follows the steps of the analysis of a field trial: fit the model of
the design, check its assumptions, compare the treatments, draw the figures and
write the report. This vignette walks through them with a maize trial: four
nitrogen rates in a randomised complete block design with four blocks.

```{r}
library(AgriDesign)
head(maize_nitrogen)
```

## 1. The analysis of variance

`design_anova()` takes the data in long format (one row per plot) and the
role of each column: the response, the treatment factor(s), the blocks (or the
rows and columns of a Latin square) and, if any, covariates. When `design` is
not given, it is suggested from the roles.

```{r}
fit <- design_anova(maize_nitrogen, response = "Yield_t_ha", treatment = "Nitrogen_kg_ha",
                    block = "Block")
fit
```

The designs that can be analysed, and the roles each one needs, are listed by
`designs()`:

```{r}
designs()[, c("id", "name")]
```

## 2. Assumptions

`check_assumptions()` runs the usual checks on the residuals and summarises
them in a grade from A (satisfied) to D (several assumptions fail).

```{r}
check_assumptions(fit)
```

Observation 16 has a studentized residual of 2.65; it is worth checking in the
field book, but on its own it does not invalidate the analysis. The residual
plots show the same picture:

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(fit)
```

When an assumption fails, `transformations()` compares the candidate
transformations on the same model and suggests one, and `nonparametric()`
offers rank-based alternatives. In the tomato factorial the block and
treatment effects are multiplicative and the logarithm removes the problem:

```{r}
tom <- design_anova(tomato_factorial, "Yield_kg_plant", c("Variety", "Fertilizer"), block = "Block")
transformations(tom)$verdict
tom_log <- design_anova(tomato_factorial, "Yield_kg_plant", c("Variety", "Fertilizer"),
                        block = "Block", transform = "log")
check_assumptions(tom_log)$grade
```

## 3. Comparing the treatments

`compare_means()` separates the least-squares means with one of eleven
procedures and labels them with letters: means that share a letter do not
differ.

```{r}
cmp <- compare_means(fit, "Nitrogen_kg_ha", method = "tukey")
cmp
```

Nitrogen rates are quantitative, so the trend is more informative than the
letters. `trend()` splits the sum of squares into orthogonal polynomial
components and fits the curve:

```{r}
tr <- trend(fit, "Nitrogen_kg_ha")
tr
```

Planned comparisons are tested with `test_contrasts()`:

```{r}
test_contrasts(fit, "Nitrogen_kg_ha", rbind("control vs fertilised" = c(3, -1, -1, -1),
                                            "120 vs 180" = c(0, 0, 1, -1)))
```

## 4. Figures

Every result has a `plot()` method, and `save_figure()` writes it at the size
and resolution a journal asks for (PNG and TIFF carry the resolution in their
header; PDF, SVG and EPS are vector formats).

```{r}
plot(cmp)
plot(cmp, style = "box")
plot(tr)
```

```r
save_figure("figure1.tiff", plot(cmp), width = 8.5, height = 6.5, units = "cm", res = 600)
```

## 5. The report

`design_report()` writes all of the above in one self-contained HTML file:
a materials and methods paragraph, descriptive statistics, the assumption
checks, the analysis of variance with a draft of the results, the means with
their letters, trends, figures and appendices. Open it in a browser and print
it to PDF from there.

```r
design_report(fit, "maize-report.html", title = "Nitrogen rates in maize",
              authors = "A. Author", units = "t/ha")
```
